newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan envoy in Belgium, may visit Africa. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Taiwan envoy in Belgium, may visit Africa. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]

text.p: Taiwan's parliament on Wednesday demanded to know the European itinerary of Foreign Minister John Chang but officials, citing pressure from rival China, would confirm only that Chang was in Belgium.
State television said Chang had been invited to address the European Parliament, which has lent moral support to Taiwan in its bitter rivalry with communist Beijing.
Foreign affairs vice minister Chen Chien-jen was sparing with details when lawmakers demanded to know more about Chang's stealthy exit for Europe late on Monday.
"Minister Chang is visiting Belgium," Chen said.
Chen declined to elaborate on Chang's itinerary or the reported European Parliament speech, saying early exposure could hurt Taiwan in its diplomatic tug-of-war with mainland China.

Beijing, which has viewed the island as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has steadily tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in a quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule. It has warned other countries not to exchange ties with Taipei or permit visits by senior Taiwan officials.
On Tuesday, Beijing said Taiwan's handful of allies would have to shut their Hong Kong consulates after the British colony reverted to Chinese rule on July 1.

Chang caught Taiwan off guard when he slipped out of Taipei just a day after brusquely severing ties with the Caribbean island nation of the Bahamas, known to be preparing to switch recognition to Beijing.
Chen said Chang's trip was unrelated to diplomatic relations and only hinted at Chang's mysterious purpose.
"The visit has nothing to do with establishing formal relations with others," Chen said. "What he's doing is something he has never done. But it absolutely is helpful in our diplomatic work."

State television said Chang was invited to address the European Parliament, which in March 1996 condemned intimidating war games that China was mounting in waters near Taiwan and demanded that Beijing halt the sabre rattling.

Beijing, suspecting a growing independence mood in Taiwan, staged eight months of war games -- including unarmed ballistic missile tests -- in what it acknowledged was a bid to influence Taiwan's historic March 1996 presidential election.
Taipei's China Times Express said Chang would travel to West Africa via France to visit unspecified countries there.

Chang's overseas trip, his eighth since becoming foreign minister 11 months ago, was seen as government efforts to break diplomatic squeeze from China. Six of his trips were unannounced so as to allow Beijing little time to interfere.
Taiwan has seen its alliances weaken in recent years. The African state of Niger switched in 1996 and South Africa, Taiwan's biggest ally, said in November it would do so in 1997.
With the loss of the Bahamas, Taiwan has diplomatic links with only 30 states, largely in Central America and Africa, most of them small, poor and heavily dependent on Taipei's financial largesse.

To avert what Chang called the "domino effect", a nightmare scenario in which one defection triggers a series, Taipei has sent senior economic officials on fence-mending missions to Africa and Central America.

A cabinet minister, Chiang Pin-kung of the Council on Economic Planning and Development, is currently visiting Latin America (corrects from "will visit Latin America in July"). President Lee Teng-hui will visit Panama and neighbouring central American allies in September.
